articles.title: Recognise magnetic interference near a walking compass
articles.summary: Nearby metal and electronics can affect a magnetic compass reading.

sections.title: Identify likely interference
paragraphs: A magnetic compass responds to the local magnetic field, not just the Earth's field. Large metal objects, magnets and some electronic accessories can distort a reading.
The effect varies with distance and object, so a compass that seems normal in one position may behave differently beside another item.

sections.title: Keep observations separate
paragraphs: When practising in a familiar, low-risk place, compare the needle's behaviour away from and near carried equipment without using that experiment to navigate.
Store the compass away from magnetic closures and check its maker's care guidance before a trip.

sections.title: Know the limit
paragraphs: An apparently steady needle is not proof of accuracy, and this guide does not teach bearings or remote-terrain navigation.
For consequential navigation decisions use appropriate training, suitable maps and independent checks rather than trusting one uncertain instrument.

visual.alt: Three stages show separating a compass from potential interference, observing its needle and checking with another appropriate reference.
visual.caption: Keep possible interference in mind when assessing compass reliability.

articles.title: Inspect a headtorch tilt hinge before routine use
articles.summary: A worn hinge may let a light point away from the intended area.

sections.title: Recognise the moving part
paragraphs: Many headtorches have a pivot between the lamp housing and its headband mount. Repeated movement can loosen the hinge or damage its stops.
Check the manufacturer's intended adjustment range; not every model has a tilting head.

sections.title: Inspect without forcing
paragraphs: With the lamp switched off, look for visible cracks, missing hinge pieces and unexpected looseness.
Move the housing only through its normal adjustment range and confirm it holds its position without pressing against a damaged joint.

sections.title: Keep lighting dependable
paragraphs: A stable hinge does not prove that batteries, seals or the light source are working; check those separately before use.
Replace a damaged mount according to manufacturer instructions instead of improvising a repair that could detach during use.

visual.alt: A checklist distinguishes the lamp housing, tilt pivot and whether the headtorch retains its intended position.
visual.caption: Inspect the mount as well as the lamp.

articles.title: Check daypack compression straps without over-tightening
articles.summary: Compression straps can secure ordinary pack contents but should not distort a bag or obstruct access.

sections.title: Understand their purpose
paragraphs: Side or front compression straps on a daypack are usually intended to reduce slack around a partly filled bag.
Their presence does not make the bag a load-rated hauling system, and strap layouts vary between models.

sections.title: Look for simple wear
paragraphs: Check webbing for frayed edges, buckles for cracks and stitching for obvious separation before an ordinary walk.
Adjust straps evenly enough to avoid dangling loops, without crushing fragile items or trapping zips.

sections.title: Avoid mistaken uses
paragraphs: Do not use everyday compression straps for climbing, towing, lifting people or supporting safety-critical loads.
Follow the maker's load and attachment guidance; replace damaged parts rather than tying improvised high-load knots.

visual.alt: A three-part checklist checks compression-strap webbing, buckle condition and continued access to bag compartments.
visual.caption: Secure the pack without creating new snags.

articles.title: Understand the role of grid lines on a paper walking map
articles.summary: A printed grid is a reference system whose spacing and labels depend on the map.

sections.title: Recognise the grid
paragraphs: Some walking maps display regularly spaced lines with numbered margins, while others use a different grid or no visible grid.
The printed grid is not necessarily the same as latitude and longitude, and its reference system should be identified from the map legend.

sections.title: Keep labels together
paragraphs: When copying a small map extract for study, retain enough margin labels and scale information to interpret its grid.
If a page is rotated or cropped, note its original orientation and edition rather than guessing coordinates from a bare square.

sections.title: Respect precision limits
paragraphs: A grid square describes an area, not an exact point, and a short reference can be ambiguous without its region or grid system.
Do not combine coordinates from different datums or projections without understanding the conversion; seek trained help for consequential use.

visual.alt: Three labelled layers identify grid lines, edge labels and the coordinate system that gives them meaning.
visual.caption: A grid reference needs its map context.

articles.title: Inspect an insulated flask lid and seal before a walk
articles.summary: A worn or misplaced seal can allow leaks even when the flask body looks sound.

sections.title: Find the sealing surfaces
paragraphs: Reusable insulated flasks may use removable gaskets, threaded lids or drinking spouts, depending on the model.
Check the manufacturer's instructions to identify parts that are meant to be removed for routine cleaning.

sections.title: Observe condition
paragraphs: Look for missing, twisted or visibly damaged seals and for cracks around the lid or threads.
Reassemble only as instructed and test with cool water over a sink before packing; a cool-water test does not certify safe use with hot contents.

sections.title: Avoid unsafe assumptions
paragraphs: Do not assume a flask is leakproof merely because the cap turns firmly, and do not use improvised sealants.
Hot liquids can cause burns if a closure fails; follow the manufacturer's temperature and handling guidance.

visual.alt: A checklist separates gasket condition, lid-thread condition and a cautious cool-water leak check.
visual.caption: Check closure integrity before packing a flask.

articles.title: Understand offline maps and phone airplane mode
articles.summary: Offline map data and satellite positioning are different phone functions.

sections.title: Separate the functions
paragraphs: A downloaded map provides stored geographic information, while satellite positioning uses signals received by the phone.
Airplane mode disables some wireless connections, but whether location services continue to work depends on the device and settings.

sections.title: Test at home
paragraphs: Before travelling, check whether the intended map area is actually downloaded and opens without mobile data.
In a familiar location, check the phone's location settings and the mapping app's offline behaviour rather than assuming a saved route guarantees map coverage.

sections.title: Keep expectations realistic
paragraphs: A location marker may be delayed or inaccurate near buildings, under tree cover or where reception is poor.
Offline maps do not provide live closures or weather updates; keep a suitable independent navigation reference for activities where a phone failure matters.

visual.alt: Three stages show downloading map coverage, testing without mobile data and checking whether the app behaves as expected.
visual.caption: Verify offline map access before depending on it.

articles.title: Inspect reflective accessories on everyday walking gear
articles.summary: Reflective trim can become obscured or damaged through routine use.

sections.title: Identify the material
paragraphs: Some bags and clothing use reflective patches, piping or detachable accessories that return light toward a source.
Reflective material is different from a light source and may be difficult to notice without illumination.

sections.title: Check visible condition
paragraphs: Inspect for peeling, heavy dirt, abrasion and loose attachments in ordinary lighting.
Clean only as the maker recommends and check that accessories do not obstruct zips, straps or normal movement.

sections.title: Understand its limits
paragraphs: Reflective details do not guarantee that other people or drivers will see you, especially in poor weather or from every angle.
Do not treat an accessory as a substitute for suitable route choice, lighting and local road-safety guidance.

visual.alt: Three checks show reflective surface condition, secure attachment and the need to understand visibility limits.
visual.caption: Reflective accessories are supplemental, not a guarantee of visibility.

articles.title: Check publication dates on walking guidebooks and route cards
articles.summary: Printed route descriptions may remain readable after their practical details become outdated.

sections.title: Find the provenance
paragraphs: Look for the edition, publication date, publisher and any stated map references on a printed guidebook or route card.
A recent printing is not necessarily a recent field survey, and a reprint may retain older route descriptions.

sections.title: Record what is known
paragraphs: Keep the edition and page reference with personal route notes so you can distinguish versions later.
Check current authoritative access and transport information before a trip where connectivity permits, especially for routes with changing restrictions.

sections.title: Do not infer current conditions
paragraphs: A printed route description cannot confirm today's path closures, bridge condition, daylight or weather.
Use the guide as historical planning context, not as a live safety notice or an assurance that a route remains passable.

visual.alt: Three labelled reference slots show edition information, original publisher and the need for current checks.
visual.caption: Keep a guidebook's publication context visible.
